title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 21: New Jurisprudence on Capital Offenses
keywords: waiver of the right to present evidence
primary_topics: Chapter 21 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's annual survey of new Supreme Court jurisprudence on capital offenses decided from October 10, 2003 to October 10, 2004, the period marking his ninth year in office

People v. Mateo as the most significant death penalty Decision of that year: Justice Vitug's valedictory ponencia requiring an intermediate review by the Court of Appeals of all heinous-crime judgments, implemented through AM No. 00-5-03-SC amending Rules 122 and 124

His six nonlegal reasons for voting with the unanimous Court in Mateo -- equal access to review, the CA's factual expertise, a decade of settled doctrine to guide it, the surviving automatic Supreme Court review, the CA's enlarged membership, and the time freed for the High Court's other work

A doctrinal roundup of the year's rulings on evidence and procedure in capital cases: DNA testing, airport searches, special complex crimes, the preamble of the Information, waivers of the right to present evidence, searching inquiries on pleas of guilty, custodial investigation, sexual assault, relationship as an alternative circumstance, pretrial stipulations, proof of age and filiation, use of explosives, and the quorum required to impose death
sub_topics: The Judicial Records Office statistics for the review period, and his observation that less than one third of capital cases reviewed since the Death Penalty Law took effect on December 31, 1993 have been affirmed -- evidence of the Court's special assiduousness

People v. Mateo: nothing in the Fundamental Law proscribes an intermediate review, and where life and liberty are at stake 'no care in the evaluation of the facts can ever be overdone'; the CA may impose the penalty but must refrain from entering judgment and elevate the records

AM No. 00-5-03-SC of September 28, 2004 amending Sections 3 and 10 of Rule 122 and Sections 12 and 13 of Rule 124, including automatic CA review without notice of appeal where the trial court imposed death
His first reason: if those charged with simple theft enjoy multiple review through the four-level judicial hierarchy, death convicts should not be denied the same privilege
His second reason: capital cases turn on facts, the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts, and the Court of Appeals is mandated and expert in reviewing factual conclusions

His third, fourth, fifth and sixth reasons: a decade of doctrine now guides the CA; automatic Supreme Court review survives by constitutional fiat and acquittals are unappealable; RA 8246 enlarged the CA to 69 justices in 23 divisions; and the High Court gains time for novel economic, Information Age and bioscientific disputes and for its Judicial Reform Program

DNA evidence: after People v. Vallejo upheld its reliability, People v. Yatar used a sperm-specimen match in a rape with homicide, rejecting the self-incrimination objection because the right bars testimonial compulsion, not object evidence

People v. Suzuki: routine airport security searches are reasonable given minimal intrusiveness, the gravity of safety interests and reduced privacy expectations, and the appellant had consented, making his warrantless arrest in flagrante delicto valid

People v. Otayde: there is no complex crime of robbery with homicide and assault upon a person in authority; where robbery is the main purpose and the killing results by reason or on the occasion of it, the offense is robbery with homicide -- and all principals in the robbery are principals in the special complex crime unless they endeavored to prevent the killing (reiterated in People v. Abes)

People v. Villanueva: the Information must be read as one whole document, so a qualifying circumstance such as relationship alleged in the preamble counts; the preamble 'is as much an essential part of the Information as the accusatory paragraph itself'

People v. Macarang and People v. Beriber: a waiver of the right to present evidence must be voluntary, knowing and intelligent, and a judge who imposes waiver as a penalty for postponements -- while also letting counsel withdraw -- cannot then sentence the accused to death

People v. Besonia: a plea of guilty is only secondary basis for culpability; a regular trial must still be held, and the three-page Decision there 'leaves much to be desired,' the prosecution 'lacking in assiduity,' so the case was remanded

People v. Mojello: the majority treated two custodial investigations separately and found the second untainted, while Justice Quisumbing dissented that the second confession was the unlawful consequence of the first, 'a classic case of a fruit of the poisonous tree'
People v. Palma: under the Anti-Rape Law of 1997, insertion of a finger into the victim's vagina constitutes consummated rape through sexual assault

People v. Orilla: relationship as an alternative circumstance cannot qualify a crime for death unless Congress expressly so prescribes; 'aggravating circumstance' is read strictly when death is at stake and broadly for civil liability, as in People v. Catubig

The tension between People v. Pepito, which appreciated minority and relationship from pretrial admissions, and People v. Balbarona, where Justice Carpio Morales held that circumstances qualifying a crime and raising the penalty to death cannot be the subject of stipulation

People v. Carpio: the 'use of a deadly weapon' aggravates rape but not the complex crime of robbery with rape; People v. Macabata, People v. Antivola and People v. Estrada on proving the victim's age; People v. Cea on a baptismal certificate as proof of filiation only when coupled with the accused's admission

People v. Comadres: where a killing is by means of explosives, that circumstance qualifies the offense and treachery becomes generic; RA 8294 lowered penalties and made illegal possession of explosives an aggravating circumstance rather than a separate offense, with Justice Callejo dissenting that treachery should qualify and the explosives circumstance be absorbed

People v. Ebio: with only seven of fourteen justices deliberating and signing, the Court recalled its Decision and resubmitted the case en banc, holding that doubt in a capital case must be resolved in favor of the accused -- though on re-deliberation with twelve justices it unanimously affirmed the death sentence

stances.claim: People v. Mateo was rightly decided: death convicts should enjoy the intermediate factual review that even those charged with simple theft receive through the four-level judicial hierarchy, and the Court of Appeals -- mandated and expert in reviewing factual conclusions, unlike a Supreme Court that is not a trier of facts -- will minimize errors of judgment.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from equal access and institutional competence, laid out in six numbered reasons in deliberately nonlegal English

stances.claim: The Supreme Court has been exceptionally careful with capital cases: less than one third of those reviewed since the Death Penalty Law took effect have been affirmed, a statistic reflecting its assiduousness in protecting the rights of the accused from arrest through trial to judgment.
stances.rhetorical_move: statistical demonstration, citing the Judicial Records Office figures before drawing the inference

stances.claim: Where the imposable penalty is death, procedural safeguards must be enforced strictly: a waiver of the right to present evidence must be voluntary, knowing and intelligent and can never be imposed as a sanction; a plea of guilty is only secondary evidence and a searching inquiry plus a regular trial is still required; and doubt about a quorum must be resolved in favor of the accused.
stances.rhetorical_move: gravity-of-penalty reasoning: a series of remands and recalls marshalled to show that the higher the stake, the stricter the procedure

stances.claim: Justice Quisumbing dissented in People v. Mojello that the second custodial interrogation could not cure the first, the confession being the unlawful consequence of an uncounselled interrogation and therefore a classic case of a fruit of the poisonous tree.
stances.rhetorical_move: reproduction of a dissent at length, presented as an unresolved division within the Court rather than as his own position

notable_anecdotes: CJP opens by placing the chapter in a personal series -- 'as in my previous books' -- and dates the survey to the period marking his ninth year in office on the Court.
He records that People v. Mateo was Justice Jose C. Vitug's valedictory ponencia, promulgated one week before the esteemed magistrate's retirement, and calls it a 'new Vitug masterpiece.'
He explains that he voted for Mateo without writing a Separate Opinion, and chooses instead to set out his six reasons in this book in nonlegal, easy-to-understand English.

He recounts the trial judge in Macarang who, annoyed by repeated postponements, declared the accused to have waived his right to present evidence, allowed his counsel to withdraw in the same Order, and then sentenced him to death.

He describes the rare episode in People v. Ebio, where only seven of the fourteen justices had deliberated and signed the Decision imposing death, leading the Court to recall its own ruling and resubmit the case for re-deliberation -- after which twelve justices unanimously affirmed the same sentence.
He notes the apparent conflict he observed between People v. Pepito and People v. Balbarona on whether qualifying circumstances may rest on pretrial admissions alone.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' surveyed the Supreme Court's new jurisprudence on capital offenses for the period from October 10, 2003 to October 10, 2004, the year marking CJP's ninth on the Court. He opened with Judicial Records Office statistics and observed that less than one third of the capital cases reviewed since the Death Penalty Law took effect on December 31, 1993 had been affirmed, a figure he read as proof of the Court's special assiduousness. The year's most significant ruling was People v. Mateo, Justice Vitug's valedictory ponencia, which held it wise and compelling to have the Court of Appeals review all heinous-crime judgments before they reach the Supreme Court, and which the Court implemented through AM No. 00-5-03-SC amending Rules 122 and 124. Having voted for Mateo without writing separately, CJP set out six reasons in plain English: death convicts deserve the same multiple review that petty offenders enjoy; capital cases turn on facts and the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts while the Court of Appeals is; a decade of doctrine now guides the CA; automatic Supreme Court review survives by constitutional fiat and acquittals remain unappealable; the CA had been enlarged to 69 justices; and the High Court would gain time for novel disputes and its Judicial Reform Program. He then reviewed the year's other rulings -- DNA evidence in Vallejo and Yatar and the limits of the self-incrimination clause, the validity of routine airport searches in Suzuki, the rejection of a complex crime of robbery with homicide and assault in Otayde, the reading of an Information as one whole document in Villanueva, the strict scrutiny of waivers in Macarang and Beriber, the searching inquiry required in Besonia, the divided treatment of successive custodial investigations in Mojello, and the rulings on sexual assault, relationship, pretrial stipulations, proof of age and filiation, explosives, and the quorum question recalled and re-deliberated in People v. Ebio.
